--- title: "The Projective Quadrume: Extending Rational Trigonometry to Tetrahedra and Higher Dimensions" author: "Math Blog" date: "2026-07-24" categories: [pure-math, universal-hyperbolic-geometry, projective-geometry, quadrea, quadrume] description: "From the projective quadrea of a triangle to the projective quadrume of a tetrahedron: a purely algebraic, recursive theory of hypervolume for projective simplices in any dimension." format: html: toc: true toc-depth: 3 code-fold: false theme: cosmo mathjax: true bibliography: references.bib --- ## From Quadrea to Quadrume: Climbing a Dimension In our earlier post on the **projective quadrea**, we watched N. J. Wildberger's rational trigonometry do something remarkable: it took the metrical geometry of a projective triangle in $\mathbb{P}^2$ — a triangle built from three lines through the origin of an ambient vector space $\mathbb{V}^3$ — and expressed every measurement as a ratio of polynomials in a bilinear form. No $\sin$, no $\cos$, no square roots, no transcendental machinery. Just a symmetric bilinear form $B$, a handful of Gram determinants, and a field $\mathbb{F}$ with $\mathrm{char}(\mathbb{F}) \neq 2$. That framework — **quadrance** for the "squared distance" between points, **spread** for the "squared angle" between lines, and **quadrea** for the invariant of a whole triangle — is the backbone of Wildberger's *Universal Hyperbolic Geometry*. It works because rational trigonometry refuses to privilege the real numbers or the transcendental functions built on them; it insists that everything metrical reduces to polynomial identities that make sense over *any* field of characteristic not two. The natural question is: what happens one dimension up? If a projective triangle in $\mathbb{P}^2$ has a quadrea, what does a projective **tetrahedron** in $\mathbb{P}^3$ have? John D. Coady's paper, *On the Projective Quadrume and the Recursive Factorization of Projective Simplices* [@coady2026quadrume], answers this directly. It defines the **projective quadrume** of a tetrahedron as a normalized $4\times4$ Gram determinant, proves that it factorizes cleanly into a face quadrea times an altitude quadrance, and then shows that this is just the first non-trivial case of a completely general recursive theorem for simplices of any dimension. This post walks through that construction. The full paper is openly available on Zenodo at [doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21523416](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21523416). ## The Algebraic Setting Everything rests on a single piece of data: an $n$-dimensional vector space $\mathbb{V}^n$ over a field $\mathbb{F}$ with $\mathrm{char}(\mathbb{F}) \neq 2$, equipped with a non-degenerate symmetric bilinear form $B(u,v)$. The characteristic restriction is not a technicality to wave away — it is what keeps a symmetric bilinear form from collapsing into an alternating one, and it keeps the number $2$ invertible, which the definitions below lean on constantly. **Quadrance.** For a vector $v \in \mathbb{V}^n$, $$ Q(v) \equiv B(v,v). $$ A vector is **null** if $Q(v) = 0$; the theory only tracks non-null representatives. **Projective points and projective quadrance.** A point $a_i$ of $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ is a one-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{V}^n$, represented by a non-null vector $v_i$. The projective quadrance between two points is $$ q(a_1,a_2) \equiv 1 - \frac{B(v_1,v_2)^2}{Q(v_1)\,Q(v_2)}. $$ **The projective Gram volume.** This is the key generalization. Given $k$ vectors $v_1,\dots,v_k$, form the $k\times k$ Gram matrix $[G_k]_{ij} = B(v_i,v_j)$. The **projective Gram volume** is the normalized determinant $$ \mathcal{Q}_k \equiv \frac{\det(G_k)}{\prod_{i=1}^{k} Q(v_i)}. $$ This single quantity unifies the whole hierarchy: at $k=2$ it *is* the projective quadrance, at $k=3$ it is Wildberger's **projective quadrea** $\mathcal{S}$, and at $k=4$ it is what Coady names the **projective quadrume** $\mathcal{V}$ — the natural continuation of Wildberger's naming scheme for the tetrahedral case. Crucially, $\mathcal{Q}_k$ doesn't care which representative vectors you chose. Scaling $v_i \to \lambda_i v_i$ multiplies $\det(G_k)$ by $\prod \lambda_i^2$ and multiplies $\prod Q(v_i)$ by the same factor, so the ratio is invariant — exactly the projective invariance you need for this to be a well-defined geometric quantity rather than an artifact of coordinates. ## Why Gram Determinants Factor: The Exterior Algebra Picture Before stating the tetrahedral theorem, it's worth seeing *why* Gram determinants factor at all, because the reason is geometric, not just algebraic bookkeeping. The Gram determinant of $k$ vectors has a coordinate-free meaning in the exterior algebra $\bigwedge^k \mathbb{V}^n$: $$ \det(G_k) = \langle v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_k,\; v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_k \rangle. $$ If you decompose the last vector $v_k = v_k^{\parallel} + v_k^{\perp}$ relative to the span of the first $k-1$ vectors, the parallel component contributes nothing to the wedge product — a wedge with a repeated direction vanishes — so $$ v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_{k-1} \wedge v_k = v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_{k-1} \wedge v_k^{\perp}. $$ This is the exterior-algebra shadow of the familiar Euclidean fact that *(squared base) $\times$ (squared height) = squared volume*. Made precise as a Gram determinant statement: > **Lemma (Gram Determinant Factorization).** If $U_{k-1} \subset U_k$ with > $\dim U_{k-1} = k-1$, $\dim U_k = k$, and $B|_{U_{k-1}}$ is non-degenerate, then > $$\det(G_k) = \det(G_{k-1}) \cdot Q(v_k^{\perp}),$$ > where $v_k^{\perp}$ is the component of $v_k$ orthogonal to $U_{k-1}$. The proof is a congruence transformation: replace $v_k$ by $v_k^{\perp}$ using an upper-triangular change of basis of determinant $1$, which block-diagonalizes the Gram matrix without changing its determinant. Everything downstream in the paper is this lemma, applied at increasing dimension and translated into projective language. ## The Dual Point of a Plane To turn "orthogonal complement of a $3$-dimensional subspace" into something computable, Coady gives an explicit cofactor construction. If $v_1,v_2,v_3 \in \mathbb{V}^4$ span a non-degenerate subspace $U$, form the $3\times4$ matrix $M$ whose rows are $v_1^T G$, $v_2^T G$, $v_3^T G$ (here $G$ is the matrix of $B$ in coordinates). The **dual point** $n$ orthogonal to $U$ is given, up to scale, by the signed $3\times3$ cofactors of $M$: $$ n_i \equiv (-1)^i \det(\hat M_i), $$ where $\hat M_i$ deletes the $i$-th column. A Laplace-expansion argument shows this automatically satisfies $B(v_i, n) = 0$ for $i=1,2,3$, and non-degeneracy of $B$ on the ambient space plus non-degeneracy of $B|_U$ together force $Q(n) \neq 0$ — the dual point is itself non-null, so it represents a genuine projective point. This is the algebraic stand-in for "the point at infinity in the direction perpendicular to a plane" — except there is no metric distance being invoked anywhere, only the bilinear form. ## The Polynomial Gram Determinant Identity With the dual point in hand, Coady states the central algebraic result of the tetrahedral case. > **Theorem (Polynomial Gram Determinant Identity).** Let $v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4 \in \mathbb{V}^4$ with > $U = \mathrm{span}(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ non-degenerate, and let $n$ be the cofactor dual of > $v_1,v_2,v_3$. Then, identically as polynomials in the coordinates, > $$ > \det(G_4)\, Q(n) = \det(G_3)\, B(v_4, n)^2. > $$ The proof combines the two previous ingredients. The Gram Determinant Factorization Lemma gives $\det(G_4) = \det(G_3) \cdot Q(v_4^{\perp})$, and the orthogonal projection of $v_4$ onto the line spanned by $n$ is $v_4^{\perp} = \frac{B(v_4,n)}{Q(n)} n$, so $$ Q(v_4^{\perp}) = \frac{B(v_4,n)^2}{Q(n)}. $$ Substituting and clearing the denominator $Q(n)$ produces the identity. The subtlety Coady is careful about is that this argument, on its face, only works where $B|_U$ is non-degenerate. But since both sides of the identity are *polynomials* in the coordinates of $v_1,\dots,v_4$ (the cofactor entries of $n$ are themselves polynomial), and they agree on a Zariski-dense open set, they must agree everywhere — including at degenerate configurations where the geometric argument alone would not apply. ## The Quadrume Factorization Theorem Dividing the Polynomial Gram Determinant Identity through by $Q(v_1)Q(v_2)Q(v_3)Q(v_4)Q(n)$ turns a statement about raw determinants into a statement about projective invariants. Define the **projective altitude quadrance** from vertex $a_4$ to the opposite face $a_1a_2a_3$ as $$ h(a_4) \equiv \frac{B(v_4,n)^2}{Q(v_4)\,Q(n)} = 1 - q(a_4, n), $$ the projective quadrance between $a_4$ and the dual point $n$ of its opposite face. Then: > **Quadrume Factorization Theorem.** For four non-coplanar points $a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4 \in > \mathbb{P}^3$ with non-degenerate face span, > $$ > \boxed{\mathcal{V} = \mathcal{S} \times h(a_4)} > $$ > where $\mathcal{V}$ is the projective quadrume of the tetrahedron and $\mathcal{S}$ is the > projective quadrea of the opposite face. This is exactly the algebraic tetrahedral analogue of *(base area)$^2$ $\times$ (height)$^2$ = (volume)$^2$, up to the appropriate normalization — except stated with quadrances and quadreas instead of lengths and areas, and valid over any field of characteristic not two, in any signature. A companion result records how the identity behaves under rescaling representative vectors: the *unnormalized* polynomial identity picks up a factor of $\prod_i \lambda_i^2 \cdot \lambda_n^2$ on both sides, while the *normalized* quadrume factorization is completely scale-invariant, as it must be for a genuinely projective statement. ## The General $n$-Dimensional Theorem The tetrahedral case turns out to be nothing special — it's the $k=4$ instance of a fully general recursion. Define the altitude quadrance of the $k$-th vertex relative to the span of the preceding $k-1$ points in exactly the same way, using the dual normal $n$ of the codimension-one face $U_{k-1} \subset U_k$: $$ h(a_k) \equiv \frac{B(v_k,n)^2}{Q(v_k)\,Q(n)}. $$ > **$n$-Dimensional Factorization Theorem.** Let $a_1,\dots,a_k$ be linearly independent points > in $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ ($k \le n$) with $B|_{U_{k-1}}$ non-degenerate. Then > $$ > \mathcal{Q}_k = \mathcal{Q}_{k-1} \times h(a_k). > $$ The proof is the identical two-step argument — Gram factorization lemma, then normalize — just carried out at general $k$ instead of $k=4$. Applied recursively down a flag of non-degenerate subspaces $U_1 \subset U_2 \subset \cdots \subset U_{k-1}$, it telescopes into a full chain factorization $$ \mathcal{Q}_k = \prod_{j=2}^{k} h(a_j), $$ expressing the hypervolume invariant of an entire simplex as a product of successive altitude quadrances — the projective, algebraic analogue of building up a simplex's volume one dimension at a time. Two caveats are worth keeping in mind. First, degeneracy: if any representative vector is null, or if $\det(G_{k-1}) = 0$ (either because the first $k-1$ points are linearly dependent, or because $B$ restricted to their span is itself degenerate), the *normalized* invariant $\mathcal{Q}_k$ simply isn't defined, even though the underlying polynomial identity still holds. Second, sign: because $\mathcal{Q}_k$ behaves as a *squared* hypervolume, it can be negative in indefinite signatures such as the Lorentzian $(+,+,+,-)$ — consistent with how Wildberger's quadrance and quadrea already handle indefinite geometries without resorting to absolute values. In the positive-definite Euclidean limit, $\sqrt{|\mathcal{Q}_k|}$ recovers (up to a fixed scaling convention) the classical Cayley–Menger volume of the simplex. ## Independent Symbolic Verification A clean way to build confidence in an identity like this — beyond the synthetic proof — is to throw a computer algebra system at it directly, with a fully general symbolic metric. Coady's appendix does exactly that: it builds four symbolic projective points, a general diagonal symbolic bilinear form (any symmetric bilinear form can be diagonalized over a field of characteristic $\neq 2$), constructs the dual point via the cofactor formula, and checks that $$ \Delta \equiv \det(G_4)\,Q(n) - \det(G_3)\,B(v_4,n)^2 $$ simplifies identically to zero. ::: {#2dd52ed6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import sympy as sp def run_symbolic_proof(): # 1. Symbolic coordinates for 4 general projective points A = list(sp.symbols('a0:4')) B_pt = list(sp.symbols('b0:4')) C = list(sp.symbols('c0:4')) D = list(sp.symbols('d0:4')) # 2. General diagonal symbolic metric (WLOG, char(F) != 2) g0, g1, g2, g3 = sp.symbols('g0 g1 g2 g3') G = sp.diag(g0, g1, g2, g3) def B_form(u, v): u_mat, v_mat = sp.Matrix(u), sp.Matrix(v) return (u_mat.T * G * v_mat)[0, 0] # 3. Cofactor construction of the dual point n orthogonal to span(A,B,C) def symbolic_dual_point(A, B_pt, C): r1 = list(sp.Matrix(A).T * G) r2 = list(sp.Matrix(B_pt).T * G) r3 = list(sp.Matrix(C).T * G) M = sp.Matrix([r1, r2, r3]) n = [] for i in range(4): M_sub = M.copy() M_sub.col_del(i) n.append((-1)**i * M_sub.det()) return n # 4. Gram matrices G4, G3 pts = [A, B_pt, C, D] G4 = sp.Matrix(4, 4, lambda i, j: B_form(pts[i], pts[j])) G3 = sp.Matrix(3, 3, lambda i, j: B_form(pts[i], pts[j])) det_G4, det_G3 = G4.det(), G3.det() n = symbolic_dual_point(A, B_pt, C) Q_n = B_form(n, n) B_D_n = B_form(D, n) LHS = det_G4 * Q_n RHS = det_G3 * (B_D_n**2) difference = sp.simplify(LHS - RHS) print("Symbolic Difference (LHS - RHS) =", difference) print("Is the identity proved?", difference == 0) if __name__ == "__main__": run_symbolic_proof() ``` ::: Running this (it takes roughly a minute or two, since `simplify` is working over sixteen free coordinate variables and four free metric parameters) prints `Symbolic Difference = 0` and `Is the identity proved? True`. This is a genuinely independent check: the symbolic computation never assumes the synthetic proof's structure, it just multiplies out sixteen coordinates against an arbitrary diagonal metric and confirms the two sides collapse to the same polynomial. ## Seeing It: An Interactive Tetrahedron The identity is easiest to trust once you can rotate a tetrahedron, drag a vertex, and watch the quadrume, the face quadrea, and the altitude quadrance stay locked in the relation $\mathcal{V} = \mathcal{S} \times h(a_4)$ no matter how you deform it. The embed below is a placeholder for a GeoGebra 3D applet illustrating exactly that: a tetrahedron $a_1a_2a_3a_4$, its base face $a_1a_2a_3$ with dual normal $n$, and the altitude line from $a_4$ to $n$. ```{=html}

Click image to launch the interactive GeoGebra 3D applet in a new window. Click and drag the points A, B, C, and D to see metric calculations update.
``` ## Closing Thoughts The projective quadrume is a satisfying instance of a pattern that shows up whenever rational trigonometry is extended: define the natural normalized Gram invariant, prove a factorization lemma using nothing but bilinear-form algebra and a change of basis, and watch the identity survive intact at every dimension. What starts as "the quadrea of a triangle" becomes "the quadrume of a tetrahedron" becomes, ultimately, a single recursive law $$ \mathcal{Q}_k = \mathcal{Q}_{k-1} \times h(a_k) $$ governing the projective Gram volume of a simplex of *any* size in a space of *any* dimension, over a field of *any* characteristic other than two. No transcendental functions were used in the making of this theorem — and that, per Wildberger's original philosophy, is precisely the point. For the full definitions, proofs, and the complete SymPy verification script, see the original paper on Zenodo: Coady, J. D. (2026). *On the Projective Quadrume and the Recursive Factorization of Projective Simplices*. [https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21523416](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21523416). ## References ::: {#refs} :::
